soil-agri-095.title: Tillage: why farmers dig, and why digging less won
soil-agri-095.text: In 1731 Jethro Tull argued that land could never be tilled too much. Tillage is the preparation of soil for farming by mechanically agitating it: digging, stirring or overturning it. By hand it means shovelling, picking, mattock work, hoeing and raking. With animals or machines it means ploughing, rototilling, rolling, harrowing and cultivating. Deeper, more thorough work is called primary tillage, and shallower, more selective work secondary. Harrowing and rototilling often do both in one pass. In farming, cultivation overlaps with tillage, but it can also mean shallow, selective tillage of row crops that kills weeds while sparing the crop. Weed control is a clear payoff. Tillage uproots weeds or buries their leaves, so they cannot compete with the crop or set seed. Tull believed soil had to be pulverized into a fine powder before plants could feed on it. Scientific observation has shown the opposite. Tillage robs soil of the structure that lets roots, water and nutrients in, speeds erosion and compacts the soil. Tilling the prairie topsoil of the American Midwest helped cause the Dust Bowl. In 2019 erosion in the United States still took an estimated 3 trillion pounds of soil. Modern agricultural science has since cut tillage sharply. With herbicides, crops tolerant of packed soil and direct-seeding equipment, crops can be grown for years without it.

soil-agri-106.title: The plough, from human muscle to the tractor
soil-agri-106.text: A Sumerian poem from the 3rd millennium BC stages a debate between the hoe and the plough over which is better. The plough, spelled plow in the United States, is a farm tool for loosening or turning over soil before sowing seed or planting. Its main work is turning over the uppermost soil, which brings fresh nutrients to the surface and buries weeds and crop remains to decay. The trenches it cuts are furrows. Ploughing and cultivating even out the upper 12 to 25 centimeters (5 to 10 in) of soil, where most plant feeder roots grow. The earliest ploughs had no wheels, a type the Romans called an aratrum. People pulled the first ploughs, then oxen, horses and mules, then steam engines, and from the early 20th century tractors. In 1837 John Deere began making polished steel ploughs strong enough for tough Midwest prairie, once thought unsuitable. A ploughed field is normally left to dry and then harrowed before planting. Where erosion threatens, shallower ploughing or other forms of {{ref:soil-agri-099}} have replaced the traditional plough.

soil-agri-126.title: Arable land, the share of farmland that can take a plough
soil-agri-126.text: In 2013 the world used 4.924 billion hectares for agriculture, but only 1.407 billion of them were arable. Arable land is land that can be ploughed and used to grow crops. FAO statistics count land under temporary crops, temporary meadows, market and kitchen gardens, and land fallow for less than five years. Land abandoned by shifting cultivation is left out. The figures record actual, not potential, use, and Eurostat defines arable land as land ploughed or tilled regularly, generally under crop rotation. Meadows, pastures and permanent crops such as orchards, vineyards and coffee plantations are farmland but not arable. Land can be unfit for cultivation through lack of freshwater, stoniness, steepness, a harsh climate, wetness that cannot be drained, or excess salts. Clay content is a major factor. Such land can still pay: about 59 percent of US non-federal pasture and unforested rangeland cannot be cultivated but is valuable for grazing. Every year {{ref:soil-env-072}} and human-induced erosion take arable land, and poor irrigation concentrates salts in the root zone. Climate change may add some back by thawing frozen ground.

soil-agri-100.title: What tillage gives a soil, and what it takes away
soil-agri-100.text: Tillage gives with one hand and takes with the other. Its effects are its consequences for a soil. On the credit side, it loosens and aerates the A horizon and mixes residue, humus and nutrients evenly through it. It destroys weeds mechanically. Autumn tillage lets frost crumble the exposed soil over winter, leaving a smooth surface for spring planting. It also cuts slugs, cutworms, armyworms and crop diseases that shelter in old surface residues. Drying the soil before seeding counts as a benefit in wetter climates, but also as a drawback. The debits run longer. Tillage breaks the cohesion between particles and destroys aggregates, the basis of soil structure. It reduces organic matter and soil life such as microbes, earthworms and ants. It tears the hyphal network of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, so the soil can infect fewer new roots. Tilled soil loses nutrients and water-storing ability, and its infiltration rate falls, so more water runs off and erodes it. Compaction into a dense layer, {{ref:soil-agri-101}}, chemical runoff and the over-enrichment of waters fed by nutrient runoff complete the list.

soil-agri-096.title: Primary and secondary tillage: rough first, fine second
soil-agri-096.text: Most tilled fields are worked twice, first roughly and then finely. Tillage divides into deeper, more thorough primary operations and shallower, often more selective secondary ones. Primary tillage, such as ploughing, loosens the soil and mixes in fertilizer or plant material, leaving a rough surface. It usually follows the last harvest, when the soil is wet enough to plough but still gives traction. The goals are soft soil to a reasonable depth, buried residues, killed weeds and aeration. Secondary tillage is any later operation. It works in fertilizer, reduces soil to a finer tilth, levels the surface, shapes rows and controls weeds. Its smoother finish is what many crops need for a good {{ref:soil-agri-116}}. The tool kit is long, from {{ref:soil-agri-114}} and {{ref:soil-agri-115}} to dibbles, hoes, shovels, rotary tillers, subsoilers, ridge- or bed-forming tillers and rollers. When the target is weeds, tools such as hoes usually disturb only the top few centimeters of soil around the crop plants.

soil-agri-114.title: The harrow, which smooths what the plough leaves rough
soil-agri-114.text: After the plough comes the harrow, a farm implement for surface tillage that breaks up and smooths the soil. A plough cuts the upper 12 to 25 centimeters and leaves furrows. The weeding tools in {{ref:soil-agri-115}} disturb only narrow tracks between rows. A harrow disturbs the whole surface, breaking clods into a tilth fit for planting seeds. Coarser harrowing can also remove weeds and cover seed after sowing. The four general types are disc, tine, chain and chain-disk harrows, and tine harrows include spring-tooth, drag and spike models. Disc harrows do heavy work, such as breaking up sod after ploughing, while chain harrows level the tilth or cover seed. Farmers commonly run a disk harrow first to slice the large clods left by the {{ref:soil-agri-109}}, then a spring-tooth harrow. The result is a smooth field with powdery surface soil. Where the tilth is very fine, or the soil light enough to blow away, a roller often goes last. The tool is old: in China the rake had developed into the harrow by the end of the Han dynasty.

soil-agri-123.title: Contour plowing: furrows that run across the slope
soil-agri-123.text: By 1938, ploughing along the contour and similar techniques had cut US soil loss by 65 percent, despite continuing drought. Contour plowing, also called contour farming, is ploughing or planting across a slope along its elevation contour lines. The level furrows run across the slope rather than down it. They form water breaks that reduce rills and gullies in heavy rain and give water time to soak in. The method also helps prevent tillage erosion, the movement of soil by tilling itself. It reduces fertilizer loss, power use, time and machine wear while raising yields. Demonstrations showed row-crop gains of up to 50% under ideal conditions, with 5 to 10% common. The Phoenicians developed contour farming and spread it around the Mediterranean, but the Romans preferred straight furrows, which became standard. The US government's soil-protection agency, set up in 1935 during the Dust Bowl, promoted it. It works only on slopes of 2% to 10% and below a certain rainfall. Steeper or wetter land adds strip cropping, and {{ref:soil-agri-073}} and {{ref:soil-agri-066}} make it more effective. In the similar practice of contour bunding, stones are placed along the contours of slopes.

soil-agri-103.title: Readying a cleared forest for new trees
soil-agri-103.text: Forests get their ground prepared too. Forest site preparation is any treatment applied to a forest site to ready it for seeding or planting. It eases regeneration by improving access, reducing or rearranging slash, the debris logging leaves, and improving poor forest floor, soil or vegetation conditions. In Ontario around 1970 the most widely used technique was mechanical scarification, using bulldozer-mounted blades, rakes, V-ploughs or teeth, or tractor-drawn scarifiers. In a British Columbia disk-trenching trial, trees on south-, east- and west-facing microsites had larger tenth-year stem volumes than north-facing or untreated ones. Overall, choosing the planting spot mattered more than the trench's orientation.

soil-agri-105.title: Mounds that give seedlings a warm, bright start
soil-agri-105.text: Five days after planting, the soil in mounds had reached a mean of 10 °C at 10 cm depth. Untreated control ground took 58 days. Mounding is a forest site-preparation treatment that builds raised planting spots, and on cold, wet sites these have improved seedling performance. Mounds warmed fastest, averaging 10 and 7 °C warmer than the control at soil depths of 0.5 cm and 10 cm. In the first growing season they had 3 times as many days with mean soil temperature above 10 °C. They also received over 4 times the daily light energy reaching control microsites.

soil-agri-104.title: Burning logging slash, and what the fire does to the soil
soil-agri-104.text: One fire can make a soil a hundred times less acidic. Slash burning for site preparation is the broadcast or prescribed burning of logging slash, the debris left on cleared forest sites, to ready them for planting or seeding. It raises soil pH by as much as 2 units, a 100-fold change, and in central British Columbia the increase persisted more than a year. The higher pH may explain copper and iron deficiencies in white spruce foliage on burned clearcuts. Phosphorus availability rose after one burn and was still higher 21 months later, but in another study it fell below pre-burn levels within 9 months. Nitrogen is lost. Burns are patchy: in one 140-ha slash burn only 4% burned severely, 47% lightly and 49% not at all.

soil-agri-102.title: How tillage wears away ancient burial mounds
soil-agri-102.text: Powerful modern tractors did as much damage in six decades as traditional farming did in the previous six centuries. English Heritage reported that finding in 2003. Tillage and archaeology meet in the damage tilling does to buried ancient remains, such as long barrows. In the UK, half of the long barrows in Gloucestershire have been damaged, and almost all the burial mounds in Essex.

soil-agri-129.title: Crop residue, the leftovers that guard the soil
soil-agri-129.text: Farmers once treated it as trash. Crop residue is the stalks, stubble, leaves and other plant material left in a field after harvest. Keeping more than 50% of it on the surface benefits soil health, nutrient cycling, erosion control and microbial activity. Surface residue softens the impact of raindrops that break up soil particles, reducing splash and sheet erosion. It cuts evaporation, lowers surface soil temperature and reduces wind effects. As it decays, it opens routes for water to soak in quickly, reducing the need for supplemental irrigation. Residue cover even defines tillage systems: under 15% for {{ref:soil-agri-097}}, 15 to 30% for {{ref:soil-agri-098}}, and at least 30% for {{ref:soil-agri-099}}. Its nutrients return slowly. Leaving residues to decay returns their stored potassium. By the next year, though, cereal straw releases only about 10 to 15 percent of its nutrients, and pea residue about 35 percent. Nitrogen depends on the residue. Above 1.5 percent nitrogen it releases nitrogen quickly; below 1.2 percent, the microbes decomposing it immobilize soil nitrogen.

soil-agri-099.title: Conservation tillage: leave the residue, keep the soil
soil-agri-099.text: Conservation tillage is used on over 370 million acres, mostly in South America, Oceania and North America. It is a group of practices that reduce tillage and leave crop residue on the surface during the critical erosion period. The threshold is at least 30% residue cover, or at least 1,000 lb/ac (1,100 kg/ha) of small grain residue. The residue slows water movement and softens raindrop impact on soil particles, so less soil erodes. Researchers found a nearly 60 percent reduction in runoff losses, and the cover also guards the surface against crusting. Fewer passes over the field save fuel and labor and reduce soil compaction. Predatory arthropods that can help control pests benefit too. Its forms include {{ref:soil-agri-117}}, {{ref:soil-agri-120}}, mulch-till, ridge-till and rotational tillage, in which soil is tilled every two years or less often. In most years since 1997 it has covered more US cropland than the more intensive systems. By 2014 more than 75% of cropland on the Canadian Prairies had adopted it. Less exposed dark soil warms more slowly in spring, which delays planting of the next corn crop. Equipment designed to cut water erosion may not reduce tillage erosion.

soil-agri-117.title: No-till farming: growing crops without turning the soil
soil-agri-117.text: Between 1999 and 2009 the land farmed without tillage grew from about 45 million hectares to 111 million. No-till farming, also called zero tillage or direct drilling, grows crops or pasture without disturbing the soil by tillage. Crops are sown into a plant cover killed with herbicide (sod seeding), through the previous crop's residue (direct seeding), or onto the bare surface (surface seeding). No-till means never tilling a field. It is one form of conservation tillage, as is {{ref:soil-agri-120}}, but the two terms are not equivalent. Organized opposition to ploughing began in the 1940s with Edward H. Faulkner's Plowman's Folly. Trials spread only after post-war herbicides such as paraquat. The area reached 72 million ha by 2003, and in 2014 South America held 47% of it. No-till cuts tillage-caused erosion, especially on sandy, dry, sloping soils. The top inch of no-till soil holds more aggregates and is two to seven times less vulnerable than ploughed soil. Surface residue helps rain and irrigation water infiltrate and limits evaporation, while each tillage pass loses around 0.85 to 1.9 cm of water to evaporation. Light-colored residue absorbs less solar energy than bare soil, so no-till soil warms and dries more slowly in spring, which may delay planting. Nitrogen immobilized in decomposing residue often reduces yields and calls for more fertilizer. After a transition, 4–5 years in Kansas, soil organic matter may build up.

soil-agri-097.title: Intensive tillage, the old conventional way
soil-agri-097.text: Speed buries residue. Faster travel with disks and deep-working ploughs, and steeper disk angles, bury more residue and so make tillage more intensive. Intensive tillage leaves less than 15% crop residue cover, or less than 500 pounds per acre (560 kg/ha) of small grain residue, on the soil. It often takes several passes with a mouldboard, disk or deep-working plough of the kind in {{ref:soil-agri-111}}. A finisher with a harrow, rolling basket and cutter then readies the ground for seed. It is often called conventional tillage, meaning the operations standard for a place and crop, which tend to bury residues. In the United States, though, conservation tillage is now more widely used, so the label is often inappropriate.

soil-agri-098.title: Reduced tillage, the middle ground for residue
soil-agri-098.text: Between the bare field and the well-covered one lies reduced tillage. It leaves 15 to 30% crop residue cover, or 500 to 1000 pounds per acre (560 to 1100 kg/ha) of small grain residue, during the critical erosion period. It may use implements such as those in {{ref:soil-agri-111}} and {{ref:soil-agri-115}}. Tillage systems are compared by percentage residue for a simple reason: the amount of crop residue left on the surface affects soil loss by erosion.

soil-agri-118.title: Does no-till really store carbon in the soil?
soil-agri-118.text: No-till cuts nitrous oxide emissions by 40–70%, depending on rotation, and that gas is 300 times stronger than CO2 and lasts 120 years. Whether no-till also raises the organic carbon stored in soil is far less certain, and the sources disagree. Many studies report more {{ref:soil-env-108}} under no-till. Others find the effect absent in some systems, depending on factors such as climate and topsoil carbon content. Some question whether measured gains are real at all, or artifacts of flawed testing methods or other factors. A 2014 study found that the no-till subsurface layer often loses more organic carbon over time than the surface gains. It called for a uniform definition of sequestration, the locking away of carbon in soil. A 2020 study found no-till combined with cover cropping stores more carbon than either practice alone. Critics add that no-till may increase herbicide use, diminishing or eliminating its carbon benefits. One cooling effect does not depend on carbon in the soil. No-till croplands have a higher albedo, reflecting more sunlight, and that cooling is similar in magnitude to other biogeochemical processes that lock carbon away.

soil-agri-109.title: The mouldboard plough, which turns the soil upside down
soil-agri-109.text: A strip of sod rolls over and lands upside down. That is the work of the mouldboard plough. Its coulter cuts down into the soil and its share cuts horizontally, freeing the strip. The curved mould board then lifts the slice and turns it over into the previous furrow. General-purpose mould boards turn the slice gently for ploughing up to 200 mm deep. Digger boards shatter it at 300 mm or more, and semi-digger boards work at about 250 mm. The heavy iron mouldboard plough was invented in Han China in the 1st and 2nd centuries and later spread to the Netherlands. It greatly cut the time needed to prepare a field, and its ridges and furrows form channels that drain the soil. Ploughing to 20 cm aerates the soil and works in residues, manure, lime and fertilizer, speeding mineralization and cutting nitrogen loss by denitrification. It raises numbers of soil-eating endogeic earthworms but deters vertical-burrowing anecic ones. It leaves little surface residue against wind and water erosion, and over-ploughing can form a hardpan. Because it was hard to turn, it changed fields from mostly square plots into long rectangular strips, hence the furlong.

openers.tillage-and-cultivation: Digging, stirring, overturning: farmers agitate soil mechanically to ready it for crops, and that work is tillage. The prize is land that can be ploughed and used to grow crops. Tilling loosens and aerates the topsoil for planting, yet it also degrades structure, speeds erosion and compacts the soil. This chapter follows that trade-off from deep primary work to shallow secondary passes, to ploughing across slopes along their contour lines, and to the stalks and stubble a harvest leaves in the field. It also visits forest sites readied for planting, and buried ancient remains such as long barrows that tilling has damaged.
